Content: Stimulated and unstimulated saliva samples have significantly different bacterial profiles. Epidemiological studies use saliva on a regular basis as a non-invasive and easy-to-take sample, which is assumed to be a microbial representative of the oral cavity ecosystem. The aim of this study was to investigate if stimulated saliva samples differ in terms of bacterial profiles compared to unstimulated saliva samples. Bacterial DNA was extracted from both types of saliva samples using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification followed by denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) profiling was performed to analyze the bacterial community structure. The results showed that stimulated saliva samples harbored a distinct bacterial community compared to unstimulated saliva samples. In particular, stimulated saliva samples displayed lower diversity and fewer bands compared to unstimulated saliva samples. These findings suggest that stimulated saliva samples might not accurately reflect the complex microbial diversity of the oral cavity and therefore should be used cautiously in future epidemiological studies.

The structure of chromosomes is studied using a technique called "banding." This involves staining the chromosomes with specific dyes that bind to different regions of the chromosome, resulting in distinct banding patterns. The two commonly used banding techniques are C-banding and G-banding.

C-banding uses a dye called CTD (Coombs' trypan blue dye) which stains DNA rich in guanine nucleotides. It produces dark bands along the length of the chromosome known as C-bands. These bands represent regions of high DNA density and are typically located near the centromere.

G-banding, on the other hand, utilizes a dye called Giemsa which stains DNA randomly. It produces lighter bands interspersed with darker bands, providing a visual representation of the overall chromosome structure. The alternating light and dark bands make up the famous "G-banding pattern" often seen in karyotypes.

By analyzing the banding patterns obtained from these techniques, scientists can gain valuable insights into the organization and composition of chromosomes. Chromosomal abnormalities such as deletions, duplications, inversions, or translocations can be identified and studied further for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

The immune system consists of two main components: the innate immune system and the adaptive immune system.

The innate immune system provides the first line of defense against pathogens and is present at birth. It includes physical barriers, such as the skin and mucous membranes, as well as cellular components, such as phagocytes (e.g., neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer (NK) cells, and complement proteins. These components work together to eliminate pathogens and initiate an inflammatory response.

The adaptive immune system is highly specific and develops after exposure to specific antigens. It consists of lymphocytes, including B cells and T cells. B cells produce antibodies that can recognize and bind to specific antigens, while T cells directly attack infected cells or aid in the activation of other immune cells. The adaptive immune system also has memory cells that allow for a faster and more efficient response upon re-exposure to the same pathogen.

Both the innate and adaptive immune systems communicate and coordinate their responses through a variety of signaling molecules called cytokines. These cytokines regulate the immune response and help to direct the immune system towards specific pathogens or threats.

Overall, the immune system plays a crucial role in maintaining the body's health by defending against harmful invaders and maintaining immune tolerance to prevent autoimmune diseases.

The null hypothesis is rejected or failed to be supported only if the study findings are highly statistically significant. The null hypothesis is not rejected just because the study findings show a trend toward a difference or association. The null hypothesis is rejected when the P value is less than the predetermined significance level, typically set at P < 0.05. The smaller the P value, the stronger the evidence against the null hypothesis.
